subtitle: The Great Tale That Burned Yet Would Not Die

panels.shot: wide, moody three-quarter shot of Gunadhya seated by a forest edge cliff, palm-leaf manuscripts piled beside him, Satavahana city shimmering in the far distance below
panels.action: Gunadhya sits cross-legged at the rim of a shadowed Vindhya forest, his face half-lit, one hand resting on a stack of palm-leaf manuscripts while, far beyond, the distant lights of Pratishthana glimmer under a dusk sky.

dialogue.text: Before Bana, before Somadeva, there was a Great Tale now lost—Gunadhya’s Brihatkatha—born in the Satavahana Deccan, burned in legend, yet shaping India’s stories for a thousand years.

i18n.hi: बाण से पहले, सोमदेव से पहले, सतवाहन दक्खिन में जन्मी, किंवदंती में जली, पर हज़ार साल तक भारत की कहानियों को गढ़ती रही—गुणाढ्य की बृहत्कथा।

panels.shot: sweeping bird’s-eye view of the Deccan plateau with the Godavari cutting through, Pratishthana marked as a bustling city by the river
panels.action: From high above, the Deccan plateau stretches like a vast brown-green sea, the Godavari river glinting as it curves past the crowded stone and timber sprawl of Pratishthana, smoke trails rising from workshops and homes.

dialogue.text: Satavahana kings ruled from Pratishthana on the Godavari, binding the Deccan’s hills and markets into one realm, as Sanskrit, Prakrit and many tongues murmured through its streets.

i18n.hi: सतवाहन राजा गोदावरी किनारे प्रतिष्ठान से राज करते, दक्खिन की पहाड़ियों और बाज़ारों को जोड़ते, और गलियों में संस्कृत, प्राकृत व कई बोलियाँ गूँजतीं।

panels.shot: interior hall mid-shot, low-angle, showing a Satavahana court with Brahmins and officials; Gunadhya stands slightly aside, holding a manuscript close to his chest
panels.action: In a pillared hall lit by oil lamps, Brahmin scholars sit near the throne reciting in measured tones, while at the edge of their circle Gunadhya, wrapped in a simple cloak, clutches a rolled palm-leaf bundle to his chest, eyes intent.

dialogue.text: Later memory placed Gunadhya in such a court, a teller at the edge of royal power, bearing a tale not in the polished Sanskrit of ritual, but in a rougher, stranger speech.

i18n.hi: बाद की यादों ने गुणाढ्य को ऐसे ही किसी दरबार में रखा—शक्तिशाली राजसत्ता के किनारे खड़ा कथाकार, जो पूजा की घिसी‑पिटी संस्कृत नहीं, बल्कि अनोखी, अनगढ़ बोली में कथा कहता था।

panels.shot: medium close-up of Gunadhya’s face, thoughtful, as courtiers blur behind him in softer focus
panels.action: Gunadhya’s face fills the frame, brows knitted yet calm, as the silhouettes of courtiers and priests behind him gesture and debate, their mouths moving silently, their forms softened and indistinct.

dialogue.speaker: gunadhya
dialogue.text: Must greatness always speak in the language of gods, never of common men?

i18n.hi: क्या हर महिमा देवभाषा में ही बोले, आम इंसानों की ज़बान में नहीं?

panels.shot: slow push-in on a stack of palm-leaf manuscripts in a dim library corner, some old, some freshly bound
panels.action: In a dim side chamber, neat piles of palm-leaf manuscripts rest on low shelves, cords binding them tight, with a few fresh leaves lying loose, their incised letters still pale on the green surface.

dialogue.text: We do not have his book. The Brihatkatha itself vanished. What we have are echoes, scattered in later pages, and a name spoken with awe—Gunadhya.

i18n.hi: उसकी किताब अब नहीं। बृहत्कथा खुद गायब हो गई। हमारे पास बस देर के पन्नों में बिखरी गूँजें हैं, और आदर से फुसफुसाया नाम—गुणाढ्य।

panels.shot: montage-style wide shot: faint, translucent figures of later authors—Somadeva, Kshemendra, a generic monk—around a ghostly central scroll
panels.action: Around a faint, glowing scroll suspended in darkness, spectral figures in different garbs—one like a Kashmiri court poet, another like a monk—face inward, each holding his own manuscript, their outlines thin and translucent.

dialogue.text: Centuries later in Kashmir, Somadeva spun the Kathasaritsagara, Kshemendra the Brihatkathamanjari; another redactor shaped the Brihatkathashlokasamgraha—all pointing back to an older Great Tale.

i18n.hi: सदियों बाद कश्मीर में सोमदेव ने कथा‑सरीत्सागर बुना, क्षेमेन्द्र ने बृहत्कथा‑मंजरी, किसी और ने बृहत्कथा‑श्लोक‑संग्रह—सब एक पुरानी महागाथा की ओर इशारा करते।

panels.shot: tight close-up of a stylized Sanskrit manuscript page, where the word 'Brihatkatha' is clearly visible in the design (but not as actual text)
panels.action: The frame focuses on a stylized manuscript leaf laid out on a wooden board, fine script rows carved across its length, with an ornamental heading suggesting the title of a Great Tale, while a hand hovers above, about to turn the page.

dialogue.text: Even Bana, in the seventh century, spoke of the Brihatkatha as something already famous, a reservoir of story that learned listeners knew by name.

i18n.hi: सातवीं सदी के स्वयं बाण ने भी बृहत्कथा को पहले से विख्यात बताया—कहानियों का ऐसा भंडार, जिसे समझदार श्रोता नाम से पहचानते थे।

panels.shot: dramatic, slightly high-angle shot of Gunadhya walking away from a city gate toward wild hills, carrying a bundle of leaves
panels.action: Gunadhya strides out through a massive wooden gate into open scrubland, a cloth-wrapped bundle of palm leaves slung across his back, while behind him the stone walls and watchtowers of Pratishthana recede into haze.

dialogue.text: Later storytellers imagined a quarrel, a refusal, a departure. Whether or not he ever walked out of Pratishthana like this, the legend insists that the Great Tale grew far from the court’s polished floors.

i18n.hi: बाद के कथाकारों ने झगड़े, इंकार और विदा की कल्पना की। सच हो या नहीं, कथा ज़िद करती है कि यह महागाथा दरबार की चमकीली दहलीज़ से दूर जाकर पली।

panels.shot: wide shot inside a dense Vindhya forest clearing at twilight, Gunadhya seated under a great tree, animals at the edge of the light
panels.action: In a forest clearing ringed by twisted trunks and hanging vines, Gunadhya sits under a vast tree with a low lamp by his side, while deer, monkeys and a curious peacock stand half in shadow at the edge of his circle of light.

dialogue.text: They say he withdrew into the Vindhya forests, that birds and beasts themselves listened as he wove a chain of stories so long it seemed to wrap around the world.

i18n.hi: कहते हैं वह विंध्य के जंगलों में चला गया, जहाँ पक्षी‑जानवर तक सुनते रहे, जब वह ऐसी लंबी कथा‑माला बुनता गया मानो पूरी धरती को लपेट ले।

panels.shot: medium shot of Gunadhya reciting with fervor, hand raised, as if addressing unseen listeners; palm leaves arranged before him
panels.action: Seated on a mat, Gunadhya leans forward, one hand lifted in mid-gesture, lips parted in speech, while in front of him rows of palm leaves lie ordered, each incised with rows of tiny characters.

dialogue.speaker: gunadhya
dialogue.text: One tale births another. Let them flow until the night itself forgets dawn.

i18n.hi: एक कथा से दूसरी जन्म लेती है। बहने दो, जब तक रात खुद सुबह को भूल जाए।

panels.shot: symbolic wide shot: a great tree whose branches hold tiny vignettes—lovers, kings, ascetics, demons—silhouetted among the leaves
panels.action: A massive tree fills the frame, its branches spreading out like a net; between the leaves hang tiny silhouetted scenes—a crowned king, a wandering ascetic, a pair of lovers, a demon with raised arms, a merchant ship on rough seas.

dialogue.text: From that lost trunk grew countless branches: adventures of princes and yakshas, of city streets and mountain shrines, of desire, renunciation and return—an ocean of narrative that later Sanskrit would long to contain.

i18n.hi: उस खोए तने से अनगिन शाखें फूटीं—राजकुमारों और यक्षों के कारनामे, नगर गलियों और पर्वत मंदिरों की झलक, कामना, संन्यास और लौट आने की यात्राएँ—कथा का ऐसा सागर जिसे बाद की संस्कृत समेटना चाहती थी।

panels.shot: close, intimate shot of a hand inscribing characters onto a palm leaf with a stylus, forest floor visible beneath
panels.action: A right hand grips a sharp stylus and gently presses into the surface of a palm leaf resting on the forest floor, thin parallel lines of freshly incised characters glowing faintly in the lamplight.

dialogue.text: Tradition calls his language Paishachi, the ‘speech of ghosts’, not the court’s Sanskrit but a wilder tongue, now mostly reconstructed from clues and arguments, its exact sound lost to us.

i18n.hi: परंपरा उसकी भाषा को पैशाची कहती है—‘प्रेतों की बोली’—दरबार की संस्कृत नहीं, बल्कि जंगली ज़बान, जिसे अब हम टुकड़ों और तर्कों से जोड़ते हैं, जिसकी असली ध्वनि खो चुकी है।

panels.shot: contrast shot: one side shows a solemn Brahmin reciting in a polished hall, the other side shows an unseen storyteller in a busy marketplace
panels.action: Split across the frame, a Brahmin stands in a pillared hall, reciting with composed dignity to seated nobles, while on the other side a shadowed storyteller gestures animatedly in a crowded marketplace, listeners leaning in close.

dialogue.text: In Gunadhya’s memory, two currents meet: Sanskrit, the ‘language of the gods’ slowly claiming prestige, and the rougher, local stories of streets and forests, in tongues later poets would call Prakrit or Paishachi.

i18n.hi: गुणाढ्य की स्मृति में दो धाराएँ मिलती हैं—देवभाषा कहलाई संस्कृत, जो धीरे‑धीरे प्रतिष्ठा पा रही थी, और गलियों‑जंगलों की रूखी‑सी देशी कथाएँ, जिन्हें बाद के कवि प्राकृत या पैशाची कहेंगे।

panels.shot: evocative mid-shot of a small fire in the forest night, with a few palm-leaf bundles set close; flames reflected in someone’s unseen eyes
panels.action: A small fire burns on the forest floor under a black sky, its orange tongues licking upward dangerously near a couple of bundled palm-leaf manuscripts, while in the foreground only the glint of reflected flames shows in a pair of watching eyes.

dialogue.text: Somadeva’s version tells of despair, of scrolls consigned to fire until the forest itself burned with stories; yet historians step carefully here, knowing how often legend loves smoke and ashes.

i18n.hi: सोमदेव का रूपान्तरण निराशा की कथा कहता है—पांडुलिपियाँ आग में फेंकी गईं, जब तक जंगल ही कथाओं से जलने लगा—पर इतिहासकार यहाँ सँभलते हैं, जानते हुए कि किंवदंतियाँ धुएँ‑राख से प्यार करती हैं।

panels.shot: wide shot of a Satavahana king on a hunt in the forest, attendants behind, pausing as he notices charred leaves on the ground
panels.action: A Satavahana king in hunting garb reins in his horse at the edge of a blackened patch of forest, attendants clustered behind him, as he looks down at a few scorched palm leaves lying amid the ash.

dialogue.text: Another part of the tale speaks of a king who found surviving leaves, who listened, wept, and brought the Great Tale back toward the city. But the chronicles of power do not confirm this rescue.

i18n.hi: कथा का दूसरा हिस्सा एक ऐसे राजा का ज़िक्र करता है, जिसने बची हुई पत्तियाँ पाईं, सुना, रोया और महागाथा को फिर नगर की ओर लौटाया—पर सत्ता के इतिहास इस उद्धार की गवाही नहीं देते।

panels.shot: symbolic shot: the fire from earlier dissolves into glowing lines that rise and transform into stylized script lines in another hand’s writing
panels.action: The frame shows rising sparks from a dying fire slowly stretching into glowing lines that curve and settle as neat rows of script on a fresh palm leaf held in a different, unseen hand.

dialogue.text: What is certain is this: even if flames once consumed his leaves, the stories did not die. They were retold, reshaped, absorbed into other texts, carrying a quiet memory of their source.

i18n.hi: इतना तो पक्का है—मान लो पत्तों को सच में आग लगी, पर कथाएँ न मरीं। वे दोहराई गईं, बदलीं, और अन्य ग्रंथों में घुल गईं, अपने स्त्रोत की मद्धिम स्मृति साथ लिए।

panels.shot: interior Kashmiri court hall wide shot, Somadeva reading his manuscript to a patron seated on a cushion
panels.action: In a richly painted hall with lattice windows, a Kashmiri poet in courtly robes sits cross-legged, reading aloud from a thick manuscript, while a patron reclines on cushions, listening with a measured, pleased expression.

dialogue.text: In eleventh-century Kashmir, Somadeva dedicated his Kathasaritsagara to soothe a troubled queen, but he carefully traced his stories back to Gunadhya’s Great Tale, honoring a Deccan lineage centuries old.

i18n.hi: ग्यारहवीं सदी के कश्मीर में सोमदेव ने अपनी कथा‑सरीत्सागर troubled रानी को शांत करने के लिए समर्पित किया, पर हर कथा का धागा वह गुणाढ्य की महागाथा तक ले गया, सदियों पुराने दक्खिनीय वंश को मान देता हुआ।

panels.shot: time-lapse style shot: shelves of manuscripts morphing gradually into printed books, then into a modern reader’s hands
panels.action: A line of palm-leaf bundles on a wooden shelf slowly fades into stitched paper manuscripts, then into stacks of printed books, until at last a pair of modern hands holds an open volume, its pages dense with English translation.

dialogue.text: Today we read Somadeva, Kshemendra, Bana. Scholars like Sheldon Pollock and Andrew Ollett trace the play of languages and memory in their words, hearing behind them the faint echo of Gunadhya’s vanished voice.

i18n.hi: आज हम सोमदेव, क्षेमेन्द्र, बाण पढ़ते हैं। शेल्डन पोलॉक, एंड्रू ओलेट जैसे विद्वान उनकी भाषा‑क्रीड़ा और स्मृति के खेल को टटोलते हैं, और पीछे गुणाढ्य की लुप्त आवाज़ की मद्धिम गूँज सुनते हैं।

panels.shot: gentle close-up of Gunadhya’s profile fading into shadow, with faint outlines of story-scenes floating behind him
panels.action: Gunadhya’s profile fills the frame for a moment—calm, distant—then his features dissolve into darkness, leaving behind only delicate outlines of lovers, kings and wanderers drifting like constellations across the black.

dialogue.text: Gunadhya’s Brihatkatha is gone, yet its ghost walks through Indian storytelling; it reminds us that even when books burn, their embers can glow on in other tongues, other texts, other ages.

i18n.hi: गुणाढ्य की बृहत्कथा मिट गई, पर उसकी आत्मा भारतीय कथाओं में चलती रहती है—याद दिलाती है कि किताबें जल भी जाएँ, तो उनकी चिंगारियाँ दूसरी ज़बानों, दूसरे ग्रंथों, दूसरी सदियों में चमकती रह सकती हैं।

subtitle_i18n.en: The Great Tale That Burned Yet Would Not Die
